title: Enraged gunman followed officers to alley; SIU probe begins after fatal battle Dead man's daughter an officer
article: A Toronto police sergeant was taking cover in a dark and narrow walkway Saturday evening when he was shot in the arm by an enraged 63-year-old man who swore he would kill police if they didn't get off his property.

Sergeant Allan Jenkins, accompanied by Constable Scott Ritchie and a third officer, was responding to a complaint of threatening behaviour at a house in the Dufferin St. and Rogers Rd. area shortly after 6 p.m. Saturday when the gunfire erupted.

After Antonio Bellon fired a single shotgun round at Jenkins, police say, Ritchie returned fire with his Glock service revolver, firing at least twice and striking Bellon in the upper chest, killing him.
Jenkins, his family at his side, is continuing to recover.
"He's got a long road ahead to recovery," said Sergeant Wylie Sheridan, a friend of Jenkins who stood guard outside the hospital room yesterday.
"He's a great guy," said Sheridan, noting Jenkins had relieved him on shift earlier Saturday. "He's well liked by everybody."

Sources close to the investigation said Jenkins used to work at Etobicoke's 12 Division with Bellon's daughter Corrine, a 15-year veteran of the Toronto Police Service. He now works out of 13 Division, to the east. "This is very hard for her, this is her father," said a senior police officer.
According to police association lawyer Gary Clewley, Ritchie, who has been on the force for seven months, is "very shaken up" by the shooting.

The investigation into the shooting has been taken over by the province's Special Investigations Unit, the civilian body charged with investigating incidents in which people are killed or injured by police.

While the SIU and Toronto police are remaining tight-lipped about details surrounding the shooting, police and other sources told the Star the incident began Saturday afternoon when Bellon threatened the owner of the Shiatsu Therapy Clinic, a business near his house.
Jenkins, responding to a 911 call from the clinic at 2019 Dufferin St., was speaking with Bellon at his back door when Bellon suddenly began swearing and produced a shotgun, witnesses said.
The three officers ducked into a nearby narrow walkway and Bellon followed, swearing. Sources say he aimed the shotgun at Jenkins and fired once.

As a wounded Jenkins dropped to the ground, Bellon continued aiming the gun. At that point, sources said, Ritchie fired at least two shots from his Glock service pistol, mortally striking Bellon twice in the upper chest.
"I hear shooting sound," said Euijong Lee, who operates the nearby Friendly Deli on Dufferin St.
Lee said he heard one shot, then a pause, then two more shots in quick succession.
From her apartment above the narrow walkway where the shooting happened, Alea, who works in the area as a psychic and uses only a single name, said she also heard a commotion.

"I heard yelling, then I heard shots," she said, adding that earlier in the day her landlord, who owns the shiatsu clinic downstairs, told her a man had been madly pounding on doors. After answering the door and being scared by the man's behaviour, the woman eventually called 911 for police assistance.
"She said he didn't make sense," Alea said. "He just said he was tired of the garbage."
During the incident, Alea said, she heard a police officer ordering a suspect to, "Stop! Stop where you are!"
The officer, Alea said, "was yelling at the top of his lungs."
The next thing she saw, Alea said, were "sparks of light.
"I knew it was gunshots."
Then she heard one officer inquiring, "Is he down? Where is he?"
Immediately after the gunfire ended, Alea said, she heard someone, believed to be Jenkins, yelling, "My arm! My arm!"

Back at his store, Lee was watching out the window when a group of frantic officers stormed up, dragging the wounded Jenkins through the door, placed him on the floor and began administering first aid.
Lee said Jenkins, who had blood on his forehead, screamed in pain when his arm was touched.
"He was screaming that it hurt," Lee said.
Louis Rigolo a neighbour of 40 years, said Bellon lost his wife two years ago and has been depressed since. Bellon visited his wife's grave almost daily, Rigolo said.
"He took it hard, there's no doubt," he said of Bellon, describing him as a "good" electronics repairman, who operated Croma Electronics, a shop at the front of his house on Dufferin St.
"All at once he closed the shop. I don't know why," Rigolo said.
Bellon was a former psychiatric patient who had been hospitalized last year, a police source said.
Although Rigolo agreed his friend had been depressed, he said "I thought he was recovering pretty good."
Just recently, he'd come over for a brandy and had been in good spirits, talking of his Christmas presents.
"Poor Tony," Rigolo said, adding he had been a good friend for many years. "Something must have set him off."
The investigation into the shooting has been taken over by the SIU. The civilian agency has named one subject officer, Ritchie, and two witness officers, including Jenkins.
"The shot officer will be a witness officer, not a subject officer," SIU director John Sutherland said.

Rose Hong, communications officer with the SIU, said investigators have interviewed some civilian witnesses and will request interviews with the officers who were at the scene. She declined to comment on the details of the shooting, explaining that such details could taint the investigation.
Coroner Dr. Barry McLellan said an autopsy was performed yesterday on Bellon. Because of the ongoing investigation, he said, "We won't be releasing information about the cause of death."
An inquest will be called into the man's death, McLellan said, but a date won't be set for that until all investigations are finished.

"It is a mandatory inquest because he was detained by police at the time." Yesterday at Sunnybrook hospital, Jenkins was surrounded by family and visited by officers who dropped by in a steady stream to see how their wounded colleague was doing.
The wounded police sergeant, who has already undergone one operation, is expected to be in hospital for at least week, according to friends, and will face further surgery.
Jenkins' wife Patricia has asked for privacy and did not wish to comment.
Jenkins, 36, survived another close call in 1988, when, as a young constable he was pinned between two cars after stopping a speeding van on Black Creek Dr. near Trethewey Dr.
The officer, who joined the force in 1986, was standing between his cruiser and the van when the car was hit from behind, trapping the officer between the two vehicles.
He suffered internal injuries and two broken legs.
Clewley, the police association lawyer, said Saturday's incident shows how dangerous the job is for police officers.
"They never know what they're going to face," he said. "This accentuates just how high the risk is for officers who go out every day and face danger in order to protect our citizens."
